title: Spotify Builds External Index to Enable Low Latency Point Queries on Its Data Lake
gist: Spotify built Random Access Parquet (RAP), an external indexing layer over Apache Parquet and Iceberg that maps keys directly to files and row locations, so online services and AI agents can do millisecond point lookups against the data lake instead of replicating datasets into Bigtable. The economic driver is stark: petabytes of online data in Bigtable versus exabytes in the GCS-based lake, making replication into serving databases increasingly untenable.

insights.claim: Spotify's Random Access Parquet lets online services and AI applications retrieve individual records directly from the data lake without replicating datasets into operational databases, keeping the same files serving analytics, ML and low-latency lookups.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: If the lake can serve operational reads, the addressable market for separate serving databases shrinks — a structural risk to key-value store revenue at hyperscalers.
insights.quote: RAP adds an external indexing layer over Apache Parquet files, enabling interactive lookups while continuing to use the same datasets for analytics, machine learning, and online serving.
insights.locator: Spotify has introduced Random Access Parquet (RAP)

insights.claim: The forcing economics are a three-orders-of-magnitude storage asymmetry: Spotify holds petabytes of online data in Bigtable while exabytes sit in its Google Cloud Storage-based data lake, so replicating lake data into serving systems is increasingly costly.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The cost gap between object storage and managed NoSQL is what funds this architecture shift; watch for the same petabyte-vs-exabyte argument at other large data estates.
insights.quote: Spotify noted that it stores petabytes of online data in Bigtable while exabytes reside in its Google Cloud Storage-based data lake, making large-scale replication into serving databases increasingly costly.
insights.locator: Spotify explained that modern data lakes have become the central repository

insights.claim: AI applications and agents are named explicitly as consumers driving the need for point lookups on lake data, alongside notebooks and ML pipelines — agentic workloads are pulling operational access requirements into the analytics stack.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Agent workloads are becoming a first-class driver of data infrastructure spend, not just a downstream consumer of it.
insights.quote: Spotify said the approach allows the same datasets to support analytical processing, machine learning pipelines, notebooks, AI agents, and latency-sensitive online applications without maintaining duplicate storage systems.
insights.locator: RAP addresses this challenge by introducing an external index

insights.claim: The bottleneck for point queries has moved off the storage device: cloud object stores now deliver millisecond access latency, so query planning, metadata traversal and file discovery dominate the remaining overhead.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Optimization effort and vendor differentiation shift from I/O to metadata and planning layers — the part of the stack Iceberg catalog vendors control.
insights.quote: Although cloud object stores such as Google Cloud Storage now provide millisecond access latency, query planning, metadata traversal, and file discovery can add significant overhead for point queries.
insights.locator: Spotify explained that modern data lakes have become the central repository

insights.claim: Distributed query engines such as Trino and BigQuery are structurally mismatched to key-based lookups because they are optimized for analytical scans, which is why an external index rather than engine tuning was the chosen fix.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Scan-optimized engines cannot be tuned into serving systems, leaving an open niche for index-layer products between the lake and the application.
insights.quote: are optimized for analytical scans rather than key-based lookups
insights.locator: Spotify explained that modern data lakes have become the central repository

insights.claim: Vikas Singh independently argued in a LinkedIn discussion that object storage performance gains have shifted point-query latency toward query planning and metadata access, corroborating Spotify's diagnosis from outside the company.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Independent practitioner agreement suggests this is an industry-wide diagnosis, not a Spotify-specific quirk — raising the odds the pattern gets productized.
insights.quote: Vikas Singh argued that improvements in cloud object storage performance have shifted more of the latency associated with point queries toward query planning and metadata access, an area that RAP is designed to reduce through precomputed indexes
insights.locator: The architecture also generated discussion within the data engineering community

insights.claim: RAP resolves a lookup key such as a user ID through an external index to a specific Parquet file and row location, then issues a targeted ranged read against object storage instead of scanning thousands of files.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: The core mechanism — key-to-byte-range resolution outside the file format — is portable to any Parquet estate and likely to be copied by competing platforms.
insights.quote: Instead of scanning thousands of files, a query resolves the key through the index before issuing a targeted ranged read against object storage.
insights.locator: RAP addresses this challenge by introducing an external index

insights.claim: The index builder generates append-only index fragments as new data lands in Apache Iceberg tables, never modifying the immutable Parquet files — preserving compatibility with the existing lake rather than forking the format.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Backwards compatibility is the adoption unlock: teams can layer this on without rewriting pipelines, lowering the barrier for a vendorized version.
insights.quote: As new data is written into Apache Iceberg tables, an index builder generates append-only index fragments without modifying immutable Parquet files.
insights.locator: RAP addresses this challenge by introducing an external index

insights.claim: Spotify layers four storage-layout optimizations on top of the index: sorting by lookup key, grouping related records, interleaving value columns for contiguous multi-attribute reads, and covering indexes that answer some queries without touching Parquet files at all.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Columnar layout assumptions get inverted for serving workloads — the interleaving trick is the non-obvious detail that makes lake-as-database viable.
insights.quote: These include sorting data by lookup key to reduce the number of files accessed, grouping related records together, interleaving value columns so multiple attributes can be retrieved through a single contiguous read, and using covering indexes that can satisfy some queries without reading Parquet files.
insights.locator: Spotify also described several storage layout optimizations

insights.claim: The explicit trade is modest increases in file or index size in exchange for fewer storage operations, with the best case being a point query served by a single ranged read of only a few kilobytes.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Trading cheap object-storage bytes for expensive per-operation latency is the underlying arbitrage; it only works while storage stays far cheaper than requests.
insights.quote: these techniques trade modest increases in file or index size for fewer storage operations, allowing some point queries to be served through a single ranged read of only a few kilobytes
insights.locator: According to Spotify, these techniques trade modest increases

insights.claim: Secondary indexes are managed at the serving layer rather than in the data pipelines, so new access paths — hash-based for exact lookups, sorted for range queries, across dimensions like buyer ID or seller ID — can be added without rewriting Parquet files or changing pipelines.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Decoupling index lifecycle from pipeline lifecycle is what makes this operationally cheap; it is the same separation that made database indexing routine.
insights.quote: Spotify said secondary indexes are managed at the serving layer, allowing new access paths without changing data pipelines while continuing to use the same Parquet datasets for both analytical scans and interactive point lookups.

insights.claim: Space-filling curve techniques — Z ordering and Hilbert curves — are cited as further levers to improve data locality for secondary lookup dimensions, extending multi-dimensional clustering from analytics into serving.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Techniques already standard in Iceberg/Delta analytics stacks transfer directly, meaning incumbent lakehouse vendors have a short path to matching this.
insights.quote: Storage layout techniques such as Z ordering and Hilbert curves can further improve data locality for secondary lookup dimensions.

insights.claim: Google Cloud has separately described an Apache Iceberg-based lakehouse architecture for AI applications aimed at the same duplication problem, but RAP differentiates by adding a dedicated external indexing layer for point lookups while staying compatible with existing Parquet and Iceberg assets.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Cloud vendors and their largest customers are converging on the same 'one copy of the data' goal — the contest is over which layer owns the index.
insights.quote: Unlike that approach, RAP introduces a dedicated external indexing layer optimized for point lookups while remaining compatible with existing Parquet files and Iceberg tables.

insights.claim: Andrew Lamb publicly framed RAP as an example of extending open data formats for interactive workloads, positioning the work as part of a broader movement to push open formats beyond analytics.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Endorsement from a prominent open-format contributor raises the chance these ideas land upstream in Parquet/Iceberg rather than staying proprietary to Spotify.
insights.quote: Andrew Lamb highlighted RAP as an example of extending open data formats for interactive workloads.
insights.locator: The architecture also generated discussion within the data engineering community
